planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted rhizome cuttings in early spring in strongly acidic, well-drained, sandy or peaty soil in full sun to light shade; velvetleaf blueberry is a cold-climate species that needs a genuinely cold winter and does not perform in hot-summer regions.

directions: Plant in strongly acidic soil (pH 4.0–5.0), well-drained and sandy or peaty, in full sun to light shade; velvetleaf blueberry is a low, colony-forming native shrub of the boreal forest and northern Great Lakes and New England barrens, distinguished from the closely related lowbush blueberry by the fine, dense, velvety hairs covering its young twigs and the undersides of its light blue-green leaves — a texture you can feel by running a leaf between your fingers. It spreads by shallow rhizomes into loose colonies and, like other lowbush blueberries, is fire-adapted, resprouting vigorously from its roots after burning or hard mowing; commercial growers of Maine's wild blueberry barrens manage mixed stands of this species and Vaccinium angustifolium on a two-year burn-and-harvest cycle for the same reason. The small, powder-blue, sweet berries ripen in mid- to late summer and are borne most heavily on wood that grew the previous year, so avoid heavy pruning right before a harvest season. Foliage turns brilliant scarlet-red in fall. Plant at least two genetically distinct plants for reliable cross-pollination and best fruit set. This is strictly a cold-climate plant, thriving where winters are long and cold; it struggles and rarely fruits well south of its native range.
